name: DICER1 syndrome
aliases: pleuropulmonary blastoma familial tumour predisposition syndrome

reference.source: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer / NCCN genetic/familial guidelines
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline pathogenic variants in DICER1, a gene central to microRNA processing, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable, often incomplete penetrance
The hallmark tumour is pleuropulmonary blastoma of early childhood, frequently preceded by lung cysts that may be mistaken for congenital malformations
The broad spectrum also includes ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour, cystic nephroma, multinodular goitre and differentiated thyroid cancer, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma and pineoblastoma
Many carriers remain unaffected, and manifestations cluster in childhood and adolescence, so age-appropriate surveillance matters
Multinodular goitre and thyroid cancer risk are increased, particularly after chemotherapy or radiotherapy for another DICER1 tumour
Tumours characteristically show a second somatic hotspot mutation in the DICER1 RNase IIIb domain in addition to the germline loss-of-function allele
Surveillance focuses on chest imaging in early childhood, pelvic and abdominal assessment, and thyroid monitoring
reference.pathophysiology: DICER1 encodes an endoribonuclease that cleaves precursor microRNAs into mature microRNAs, which fine-tune the expression of many genes controlling growth and differentiation. In this syndrome a germline loss-of-function variant is combined with a characteristic somatic missense mutation in the RNase IIIb catalytic domain of the other allele, a distinctive two-hit mechanism that selectively impairs processing of one class of microRNAs. The resulting imbalance in microRNA regulation disrupts developmental control of susceptible tissues, giving rise to the diverse embryonal and mesenchymal tumours that define the condition.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation without a germline predisposition
Sporadic Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour or cystic nephroma
additionalInvestigations: Germline DICER1 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis
Chest imaging in early childhood to detect lung cysts and pleuropulmonary blastoma
Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound for renal and ovarian tumours
Thyroid ultrasound surveillance and clinical examination for goitre
Tumour testing for the characteristic RNase IIIb hotspot mutation to support the diagnosis
Neuroimaging where pineoblastoma or intracranial disease is suspected
redFlags: Respiratory distress or a cystic or solid lung lesion in a young child
A pelvic or abdominal mass suggesting ovarian or renal tumour
A rapidly enlarging or suspicious thyroid nodule
Neurological signs raising concern for pineoblastoma or other intracranial tumour
reference.prognosis: Penetrance is variable and many carriers stay healthy, but pleuropulmonary blastoma can be aggressive, so early detection through surveillance improves outcomes. Most other tumours are treatable when identified early, and long-term thyroid monitoring is warranted given the increased malignancy risk, particularly after cancer therapy.
pitfalls: Dismissing childhood lung cysts as benign congenital lesions and missing early pleuropulmonary blastoma
Overlooking the diagnosis because of incomplete penetrance and an unremarkable family history
Failing to monitor the thyroid, especially after chemotherapy or radiotherapy
Not offering cascade testing and paediatric surveillance to at-risk relatives
references: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
management: DICER1 syndrome itself is not treated; management is lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance for component tumours plus tumour-specific treatment when a lesion is found
Chest imaging in early childhood to detect lung cysts and pleuropulmonary blastoma before progression to more aggressive solid or sarcomatous forms
Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound surveillance for cystic nephroma and ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour
Thyroid ultrasound and clinical exam for multinodular goitre and differentiated thyroid cancer, continued into adulthood and intensified after any prior chemotherapy or radiotherapy
Neuro-imaging when pineoblastoma or other intracranial disease is clinically suspected
Cascade genetic testing of at-risk relatives once a germline pathogenic variant is identified in an index case

Pleuropulmonary blastoma managed with surgical resection, adding systemic chemotherapy for higher-risk solid or mixed solid-cystic subtypes, while purely cystic type I lesions may be managed with resection and surveillance alone
Radiotherapy for pleuropulmonary blastoma used selectively given the syndrome's elevated risk of treatment-related second malignancy
Ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour and cystic nephroma managed primarily with organ- or fertility-sparing surgery, reserving systemic therapy for higher-grade or advanced disease
Thyroid nodules or cancer managed with lobectomy or thyroidectomy per standard thyroid cancer principles when malignancy is confirmed or strongly suspected; benign goitre can be followed clinically

Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma and pineoblastoma arising in this syndrome are treated with the same multimodal surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy principles used for sporadic cases, adapted to the patient
Radiation exposure should be minimised across tumour types where alternatives exist, given the syndrome's inherent susceptibility to treatment-related malignancy
Continued age-appropriate surveillance imaging persists after treatment of an index tumour since carriers remain at risk for additional unrelated DICER1 tumours
Refer to medical genetics for germline testing and cascade screening, and to a multidisciplinary team for coordinated surveillance and treatment of each component tumour
